opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the evaluation function is really the heart of the whole thing. In AlphaEvolve, the language models propose changes to code, but what turns that into a discovery process rather than just generation is having a reliable, automatic way to say "this candidate is better than that one." That's what lets you run the evolutionary loop at scale, keep the promising ideas, discard the bad ones, and build on progress over many iterations.

So far we've focused on problems where that evaluation is quite crisp: you can run the code and measure something objective. How fast is this kernel? How many scalar multiplications does this matrix multiplication algorithm use? What's the bound you get on some mathematical construction? Those settings are great because the system can't fool itself. If the number goes up, it really went up.

Going forward, I see a few directions. One is expanding the set of problems where we can write good evaluators, and a lot of that is about people with domain expertise framing their problems so they're machine-checkable. Often that framing step is where much of the human insight goes, and it's surprisingly powerful once you get it right.

Another is moving toward evaluations that are softer or more expensive, where you might combine cheap proxies with occasional expensive checks, or use cascades so that only the most promising candidates get the full, costly evaluation. In science, the real evaluation might be a simulation or even a wet-lab experiment, so being smart about where you spend your evaluation budget becomes really important.

And then there's the question of using models themselves as part of the evaluator, judging things like simplicity, elegance, or plausibility where there isn't a clean numeric score. That opens up a lot of new domains, but you have to be careful, because once the evaluator can be gamed, the search will find a way to game it. So I think the art will be combining learned judgment with grounded, verifiable signals wherever possible.

Overall, I'd say the evaluation function is becoming the main interface between the human and the system. You describe what "better" means, and the agent figures out how to get there. The better we get at expressing "better," the broader the set of discoveries these agents can make.

r001.rationale: The response says precise evaluators enable iterative progress, but does not state that this lets the agent find solutions beyond what humans have achieved.

r002.rationale: It proposes using models as evaluators for qualities such as simplicity, elegance, or plausibility when no clean numeric score exists.

r003.rationale: It mentions proxies and costly checks, but does not say that imperfect evaluators can support meaningful progress when their assessments correlate with the true objective.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the evaluation function is really the heart of the whole thing, and that's maybe underappreciated. In AlphaEvolve, the language model is proposing changes to code, but what actually drives the search is the signal you get back from evaluating those proposals. If you can write down a function that scores a candidate solution automatically, then you've turned a vague research question into something an evolutionary loop can grind away at. And the nice thing is that the system is agnostic about what that function is. It could be checking whether a matrix multiplication algorithm is correct and counting scalar multiplications, or measuring the throughput of a scheduling heuristic in a datacenter, or computing how well a geometric construction packs into some region. The same machinery works across all of those.

Where I see this evolving is in a few directions. The first is that right now the human still has to write the evaluator, and that's a real bottleneck. It requires someone who understands the problem deeply enough to say, this is what better means, and to make it cheap enough to run thousands or millions of times. I think over time the models themselves will take on more of that. You can imagine an agent proposing not just solutions but proxy metrics, intermediate signals, cheaper approximations of an expensive evaluation, and then checking those proxies against the real thing. That's a sort of meta-level loop.

The second direction is richness. A single scalar score is a fairly blunt instrument. A lot of what made AlphaEvolve work on hard problems was giving the model more than one number, so it could see which aspect of a solution was weak and reason about why. I expect evaluators to return more structured feedback, almost like a code review, and the models to get better at using that.

And the third, which I find the most interesting, is the boundary between what's verifiable and what isn't. The reason this approach has been so effective in mathematics and algorithm design is that correctness is checkable. You can't fool the evaluator. As soon as you move to domains where the evaluation is itself a judgment call, you're back to relying on the model's own taste, and that's a much weaker signal. So I think a lot of the progress in discovery agents will come from expanding the set of problems where we can construct a genuinely trustworthy evaluation, rather than from the proposal side alone. The proposer is already quite strong. The evaluator is what keeps it honest.

r001.rationale: It says an automatic evaluator lets an evolutionary loop search and that trustworthy evaluation can expand the problems agents tackle, but does not state that this enables solutions beyond what humans have achieved.

r002.rationale: It suggests models could propose proxy metrics and cheaper approximations, but does not propose using models to evaluate candidate solutions in tasks that lack precise evaluation functions.

r003.rationale: It mentions proxies and approximations checked against the real evaluation, but does not state that search can make meaningful progress when an imperfect evaluator correlates with the true objective.

astra-6.text:
I think evaluation becomes an increasingly central part of how you build these systems. In a discovery agent, you’re searching over possible solutions, and the evaluator is what tells you whether you’re actually making progress. So the quality of that signal really determines what the system can discover.

The easiest cases are ones where you can check correctness and measure performance automatically. But even there, specifying what you care about can be surprisingly subtle. If you optimize runtime on a particular set of inputs, are you finding a better algorithm, or something that happens to work well on those inputs?

I expect evaluators to become more layered: cheap checks to filter candidates, more expensive tests for promising ones, and independent validation before you trust a result. Models can help propose tests or identify weaknesses in an evaluation, too. But you still need some grounding outside the model’s own judgment.

That also changes the human role. Instead of designing every candidate solution, you spend more effort defining the problem and making sure that a higher score really means a better solution.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluator quality affects what a discovery agent can discover, but does not state that constructing a precise evaluator enables solutions beyond human achievements.

r002.rationale: It says models can propose tests or identify weaknesses in an evaluation, but does not propose using language models to evaluate candidate solutions when precise evaluation functions are unavailable.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss evolutionary search making progress with imperfect evaluators whose assessments correlate with the true objective.

sol-6.1.text:
I think evaluation is going to become an increasingly central part of how we build these agents. If you have a way to reliably measure whether a candidate solution is better, you can give the agent a lot of freedom in how it searches. It can try ideas that you wouldn’t necessarily have thought to try yourself, and the evaluator provides the feedback that guides that process.

But designing that evaluator can be the hard part. For a mathematical problem, you might be able to check correctness quite precisely. For an algorithm, you might care about correctness and runtime across a range of inputs. As you move toward more open-ended scientific discovery, the feedback can become expensive, noisy, or delayed. You may actually need to run an experiment.

So I expect evaluation to become more layered: cheap checks to filter out candidates, more expensive tests for the promising ones, and ultimately validation against the thing you actually care about. Agents can help develop those evaluations, too. But you still need an independent way to establish that an improvement is real. Otherwise, you risk getting very good at optimizing a score without making progress on the underlying problem.

r001.rationale: It says reliable evaluation lets agents explore ideas humans might not have tried, but does not state that this enables solutions beyond those humans have achieved.

r002.rationale: It says agents can help develop evaluations, but does not propose that language models evaluate candidates when precise evaluation functions are unavailable.

r003.rationale: It discusses noisy or delayed feedback and layered evaluation, but does not say evolutionary search can make progress with imperfect evaluators that correlate with the true objective.
